conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you were directly admitted for epigastric abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s that same burning pain up high again. I get nauseated and I throw up if I try to take anything by mouth. I’m scared the ulcer is back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense given your history after the Roux-en-Y and the prior gastrojejunal ulcer. Any fevers, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No chest pain. Just the stomach pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are your tube feeds going at home—were you able to tolerate them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube feeds have been okay. I’ve been putting my meds through the tube too. It’s just anything by mouth that sets me off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. For tonight, we’ll keep you nothing by mouth to rest your stomach, continue tube feeds, give IV fluids, and start an IV proton pump inhibitor to reduce acid. We’ll also treat pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to do a scope right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily tonight. First we’ll stabilize symptoms and check labs. If you don’t improve or there are concerning signs, we’d escalate. Given you’ve had similar episodes, we’ll monitor closely and coordinate next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried because I overdid it on vacation—walking a lot, not resting. Could that have triggered this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Overexertion and changes in routine can worsen nausea and abdominal discomfort, especially with your altered anatomy and prior ulcer history. It doesn’t prove an ulcer, but it can contribute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll draw blood work now—blood counts, electrolytes, kidney function, and pancreatic and liver enzymes—to make sure there’s no dehydration or other issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to end up back here again and again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal this admission is symptom control and making sure you can safely continue nutrition through the G-tube, then set you up with a plan to prevent flares as much as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is getting worse. Can I have something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s give ondansetron for nausea. For pain, we can use IV morphine as needed while we get things under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morphine makes me sleepy. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sleepiness is common. We’ll use the lowest effective dose and monitor your breathing and alertness. We’ll also work toward switching to oral pain medicine through the tube when you’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial labs are back and overall reassuring: white blood cell count is normal, kidney function and electrolytes look okay, and lipase is normal. That supports treating this as a flare of upper abdominal pain and nausea rather than something like pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it could still be an ulcer though, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it could. Labs don’t rule an ulcer in or out. That’s why we’re treating with a strong acid-suppressing medicine and watching your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t take NSAIDs anyway. I’m allergic. I haven’t taken any.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know—and we’ll avoid NSAIDs and aspirin here as well. Those can worsen ulcers even without an allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting? How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting since the nausea medicine. Pain is still there but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll continue IV fluids and the IV PPI today. We’ll keep you NPO by mouth and continue tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I at least sip water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we want to fully rest your stomach since even small sips have been triggering vomiting. We’ll reassess as symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube site looks okay, but I’m always worried it’s going to get infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked it this morning—no redness, swelling, or drainage. Keep the area clean and dry. If you notice foul-smelling drainage or increasing redness, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to review your home meds to make sure we continue them appropriately—fluoxetine and aripiprazole for mood, atorvastatin, iron, multivitamin, and your lansoprazole. You’ve also been on rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Please don’t stop my psych meds—I get really anxious if they’re missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll continue them, and we can give them through the G-tube if you’re not taking anything by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain comes in waves. Is that normal with this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. With irritation at the upper stomach or the connection after bypass, symptoms can fluctuate. The key is whether the overall trend is improving and whether you can tolerate tube feeds without worsening nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How are you feeling today compared with admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than day one. Still tender, but I’m not throwing up. I’m just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep the same plan today—IV PPI, IV fluids as needed, nausea meds as needed, and pain control. We’ll also start thinking about transitioning off IV pain meds as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home still not eating by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, yes. If your symptoms are controlled and you’re meeting nutrition through the tube, it can be safest to stay NPO by mouth for a bit. We’ll give you clear instructions for tube feeds and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about my liver—someone told me I have fatty liver. Is that causing this pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fatty liver is something we track over time, but it usually doesn’t cause sudden severe epigastric pain with vomiting like you had. Right now, your symptoms fit better with irritation or ulcer-type pain after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your nausea this afternoon? Any need for ondansetron?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used it once. It helped. I’m scared to move around too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Gentle walking is okay and can help prevent complications like blood clots, but don’t push yourself. We’ll aim for moderate activity as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today we’re going to continue your tube feeding regimen and make sure you’re tolerating it well. Nutrition will also check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed the feed rate is different than at home. Why did it change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sometimes adjust the rate in the hospital to match tolerance and hydration needs. Before discharge, we’ll set a clear home plan—right now we’re targeting a continuous rate that you tolerate without worsening symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is lower today. Do I still need IV morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you’re improving, we can reduce it and switch to pain medicine you can take through the tube or by mouth when appropriate. The goal is to control pain without making you overly sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about going home and having this come back overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We won’t discharge you until symptoms are clearly improving and you’re stable on a plan you can do at home—tube feeds, nausea medicine as needed, and a pain plan with clear return precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any vomiting today? Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Just mild nausea. Pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re on hospital day 4, and it looks like you’ve had significant improvement—less pain, no vomiting, and you’re tolerating tube feeds. How do you feel about going home later today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved, but nervous. What exactly will I do at home—still nothing by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The discharge plan is nothing by mouth for now, and continue tube feeds continuously at 50 cc per hour. That gives your upper GI tract time to settle while you still get nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds—same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume your home medications: lansoprazole twice daily, rifaximin, fluoxetine, aripiprazole, atorvastatin, iron, multivitamin, bisacodyl, mupirocin ointment, and zolpidem at night. You’ll also have ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any new medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—an oxycodone prescription for breakthrough pain. It can cause drowsiness, so no driving or operating machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like taking opioids. What if I can manage without it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. It’s prescribed as needed, not scheduled. If your pain is controlled without it, you don’t have to take it. But it’s there if pain spikes and you need something stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call your surgeon if you have fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain—especially if not relieved by medication—severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, inability to tolerate tube feeds, or any concerning drainage or redness around the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I exercise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You may resume moderate exercise at your discretion—listen to your body and avoid overexertion, especially given this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave, any last questions about the tube feed rate, medications, or follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—tube feeds at 50 an hour continuously, nothing by mouth, and keep taking the lansoprazole twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And use ondansetron for nausea as needed, and oxycodone only if pain breaks through. We’ll send you home ambulatory and stable, and you’ll follow up with your surgical team as arranged.
